record.original_question: Consider the finite triangular-grid regions called (a,b)-benzels, tiled by five trihex prototiles: a right-pointing stone, a left-pointing stone, and three bone orientations. Let T003(a,b) count tilings that allow no stones and all three bone orientations. For k >= 2, what exact formula governs T003(k(3k-1)/2, k(3k+1)/2)? More weakly, is there a recurrence or other counting method that is substantially more efficient than brute-force enumeration for these bone-only benzels?

evidence.quote: Figure 4: The five prototiles: the right stone, the left stone, the vertical bone, the rising bone, and the falling bone.
Prior to the conference, I was able to show that if an (a, b)-benzel can be tiled by bones alone, then we must have a = k(3k - 1)/2 and b = k(3k + 1)/2 (or vice versa) for some k >= 2.

Problem 1: Find an exact formula for T003 (k(3k - 1)/2, k(3k + 1)/2). Of course, even short of an exact formula, any method of determining the number of tilings that is more efficient than brute-force enumeration (e.g., a recurrence relation) would be of interest.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the triangular grid in the plane and, within it, the family of finite regions known as (a,b)-benzels (parameters a,b are positive integers; an (a,b)-benzel is the roughly hexagonal region in the triangular lattice with side-length parameters a and b, as introduced in the combinatorics of stones-and-bones tilings). The benzel is to be tiled with the following five trihex prototiles, each made of three unit triangles/hexagonal cells:
  (1) a right-pointing stone,
  (2) a left-pointing stone,
  (3) a vertical bone,
  (4) a rising (NE–SW) bone, and
  (5) a falling (NW–SE) bone.

For a subset S of these five prototiles, let T_S(a,b) denote the number of tilings of the (a,b)-benzel that use only tiles from S. In particular, write T003(a,b) for the number of tilings that use no stones and may use all three bone orientations.

It is known that T003(a,b) can be nonzero only when {a,b} = {k(3k-1)/2, k(3k+1)/2} for some integer k ≥ 1 (a pair of consecutive generalized pentagonal numbers), and that for every such k at least one such tiling exists.

Problem. For integers k ≥ 2, determine an exact closed-form formula for
    T003( k(3k-1)/2, k(3k+1)/2 ).
Failing that, exhibit any method—such as a recurrence relation or transfer-matrix approach—of computing this sequence that is asymptotically substantially more efficient than brute-force enumeration of all bone-only tilings.
artifact.status_search_result: Kim and Propp (Electron. J. Combin. 30(3) (2023), #P3.26, "A pentagonal number theorem for tribone tilings") proved that a bone-only tiling of an (a,b)-benzel exists iff {a,b} = {k(3k-1)/2, k(3k+1)/2}, settling existence. However, exact enumeration of these tilings remains unresolved: Propp's benzel-tilings problems page (last updated 2025) still lists Problem 1 (an exact formula or efficient recurrence for T003 at the pentagonal-number parameters) as "Open."

status_evidence.title: Jim Propp's Benzel Tilings Site
status_evidence.claim: Propp's official benzel-tilings problem page lists Problem 1 (exact formula or efficient recurrence for T003 at paired pentagonal numbers) as still open.

status_evidence.title: A Pentagonal Number Theorem for Tribone Tilings (Kim–Propp)
status_evidence.snippet: A benzel can be tiled by tribones iff {a,b}={k(3k+1)/2, k(3k-1)/2}; at least one tiling exists in that case.
status_evidence.claim: Existence of bone-only tilings is settled exactly for paired pentagonal-number parameters, but counting them is not addressed.
